content: Neuroleptic drugs that strongly block D-2 dopamine receptors have traditionally been used to treat tics in individuals with Tourette Syndrome. Among these, pimozide has been the most extensively studied. However, the use of such medications has been decreasing due to concerns about their side effects, and newer atypical neuroleptics have become available. The precise benefits and risks of pimozide compared to other drugs remain unclear. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness and potential harms of pimozide in comparison to placebo or other medications for managing tics in Tourette Syndrome. To gather relevant data, researchers cross-referenced the term pimozide and its brand names with Tourette Syndrome and related terms, using both MeSH headings and text words. They searched multiple databases, including the Cochrane Movement Disorders Group Trials Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE (from 1950 to April 2007), and EMBASE (from 1980 to April 2007). Additionally, reference lists of relevant articles were reviewed to identify further trials. The review included all randomized, controlled, double-blind studies that compared pimozide to placebo or other medications for treating tics in Tourette Syndrome. Both parallel-group and crossover studies involving children or adults, regardless of dosage or treatment duration, were considered eligible. Data extraction was performed independently by two authors using standardized forms, and any disagreements were resolved through discussion. Six randomized controlled trials were included in the review, involving a total of 162 participants aged between 7 and 53 years. Pimozide was compared to placebo and haloperidol in two trials, to placebo alone in one trial, to haloperidol alone in one trial, and to risperidone in two trials. The methodological quality of all studies was rated as fair. Different scales were used across studies to measure tic severity and adverse effects, leading to significant clinical heterogeneity, which made meta-analysis inappropriate. Pimozide was found to be more effective than placebo in three studies, although one of these studies reported more side effects with pimozide compared to placebo. When compared to haloperidol, pimozide was less effective in one of three studies, while the other two studies found no significant difference in efficacy between the two drugs. However, pimozide was associated with significantly fewer side effects than haloperidol. No significant differences in efficacy or side effects were observed between pimozide and risperidone. The authors concluded that pimozide is an effective treatment for tics in Tourette Syndrome. However, the number of trials comparing pimozide to placebo and other drugs is limited. Longer-term studies, lasting at least six months, are needed to evaluate the sustained effects of pimozide compared to atypical neuroleptics. Future trials should use the Yale Global Tic Severity Scale as the primary outcome measure and assess adverse events using the Extrapyramidal Symptoms Rating Scale.
